claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at% Cu to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy increases its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 5 at% Cu raises the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Stronger Cu–P interactions enhance chemical and topological frustration.
The baseline (FeCoNiCr)0.8P0.2 alloy can be produced as an amorphous ribbon or casting at a cooling rate of approximately 10^5 K/s.
The intervention replaces 2.5 at% Fe and 2.5 at% Ni with 5 at% Cu.
The proposed intervention yields the nominal composition (FeCoNiCr)0.75Cu0.05P0.20.
The beneficial Cu effect applies to alloys containing 10–25 at% P when quenched at 10^4–10^6 K/s.
The beneficial effect diminishes when P content is below 10 at%.
The beneficial effect diminishes when the cooling rate is below approximately 10^3 K/s.
Cu contents above 10 at% may reverse the effect by promoting Cu-rich crystalline phases.
Cu addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Cu and P have a negative mixing enthalpy that favors strong Cu–P association.
Cu addition produces locally favored Cu–P clusters dispersed through the amorphous matrix.
Cu–P bonding and increased size mismatch slow the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Slower crystallization kinetics increase the crystallization onset temperature, T_x.
The 5 at% Cu alloy will have approximately twice the critical casting thickness of the undoped baseline, increasing from about 0.5 mm to about 1 mm.
The 5 at% Cu alloy will exhibit a 15–25 K increase in the supercooled-liquid interval ΔT_x = T_x − T_g relative to the undoped baseline.

contradictions.description: Replacing 2.5 at% Fe and 2.5 at% Ni in the stated equiatomic baseline gives Fe17.5Co20Ni17.5Cr20Cu5P20, whereas the stated formula (FeCoNiCr)0.75Cu0.05P0.20 conventionally gives Fe18.75Co18.75Ni18.75Cr18.75Cu5P20. Thus the prose substitution and nominal formula specify different modified alloys.
